source: Vygotsky (1978) Mind in Society, ch. 6 Interaction between learning and development (quoted via secondary page)
finding: The ZPD is the gap between what a child does alone and what the child does with adult guidance. It marks functions that are still maturing, not finished ones.
numbers: Pages cited on source: 86, 88, 89-90 of the 1978 Harvard edition. No experiment; a theoretical claim.
quote: the level of potential development as determined through problem solving under adult guidance
limits: Quotes only; the secondary page did not show the mental-age example. Original text not opened.
agent_relevance: Capability is two numbers per task: solo level and assisted level. The useful target for help is the gap.

source: Vygotsky (1978) Mind in Society, ch. 6 Interaction between learning and development (imitation claim)
finding: Children can imitate actions well beyond their solo ability. So assisted performance reveals what is about to be learned.
numbers: None (theory).
quote: Children can imitate a variety of actions that go well beyond the limits of their own capabilities.
limits: Imitation limit is not quantified. Vygotsky offers no formal model.
agent_relevance: A demonstration in context can lift a model above its solo level; test how far with held-out items.

source: Vygotsky mental-age example (Thought and Language, 1986 ed. p.103), via search result
finding: Two children test at mental age 8. Given harder problems with slight help, their reached levels differ, and that gap, not the static score, is the zone. The textbook version says one reaches about 12 and the other about 9.
numbers: Mental age 8 confirmed by search snippet; the 12 versus 9 figures are recalled from memory, not verified this session.
limits: Original not opened. Unverified numbers.
agent_relevance: Two agents with equal solo score can differ in how much a lesson helps. Measure assisted gain, not only solo accuracy.

source: Wood, Bruner & Ross (1976) The role of tutoring in problem solving
finding: Pyramid-building task: an adult tutor taught children to assemble 21 interlocking blocks. Tutors began with verbal help and moved to hands-on help only if needed. This paper coined scaffolding.
numbers: 30 children, ages 3, 4 and 5, equal groups. Secondary page reports unassisted success of about 10%, 50%, 75% by age, and that tutors intervened directly twice as often with 3-year-olds as with 4-year-olds and four times as often as with 5-year-olds.
limits: Numbers come from a secondary study note, not the paper (Wiley blocked, PubMed has no abstract). Treat as approximate. Small, middle-class, one task, no no-tutor control.
agent_relevance: Tutor help should start light and escalate only on failure. That fits our rule: help from outcome signals, not on a schedule.

source: Wood, Bruner & Ross (1976) The role of tutoring in problem solving: six tutor functions
finding: Six functions: recruit interest, reduce degrees of freedom, keep direction, mark critical features, control frustration, demonstrate.
numbers: Six functions, one task.
limits: Source page words them as engaging, simplifying, maintaining focus, highlighting, managing frustration, demonstrating. Stone (1998) confirms highlighting, reducing choices, controlling frustration.
agent_relevance: Maps to lesson slots in memory: simplify, flag the critical feature, demo. A stored lesson should say which function it serves.

source: Wood, Bruner & Ross (1976) The role of tutoring in problem solving: comprehension ahead of production
finding: Children could recognise a correct construction before they could produce it. Tutor help was fitted to that gap.
numbers: All age groups told correct from incorrect constructions; no 3-year-old assembled the four-block set correctly, all 4- and 5-year-olds did at least once.
limits: Secondary source; recognition test details not seen.
agent_relevance: Checking is easier than generating. Use checks to trigger help.

source: Stone (1998) The metaphor of scaffolding: its utility for the field of learning disabilities
finding: Scaffolding was adult help so a child can finish a task beyond solo reach, with the aim of changing understanding so less help is needed later. Stone criticises the metaphor as adult-centred, too focused on gradual accumulation, and unclear on how learning happens. He keeps it and adds intersubjectivity, graduated assistance and transfer of responsibility.
numbers: No numbers (conceptual review). Read first 100,000 of 126,876 characters.
limits: Unclear whether scaffolding explains learning or only describes it. Little work on children with learning disabilities.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a lesson that helped once teaches the model. Test whether help can later be removed (fading).

source: Cazden (1979) link of scaffolding to ZPD, per search-result summary
finding: Scaffolding (Wood/Bruner) and ZPD (Vygotsky) were tied together later. They were not one theory from the start.
numbers: None.
limits: Only a search snippet said Cazden first made the link. Not verified.
agent_relevance: Keep the two ideas separate: ZPD measures readiness, scaffolding is a method of help.

source: Belland, Walker, Kim & Lefler (2017) Synthesizing results from empirical research on computer-based scaffolding in STEM education
finding: Computer-based scaffolding improves cognitive outcomes. The effect did not depend on whether the scaffold faded or added, nor on the rule for changing it. Effect was largest at the principles level and for adults.
numbers: 144 experimental studies, 333 outcomes. Random-effects mean g = 0.46. Above zero in all age groups and assessment levels.
quote: scaffolding is a highly effective intervention across levels of different characteristics
limits: Fading and customisation did not matter, which challenges a core scaffolding claim. Heterogeneous; STEM problem-centred curricula only.
agent_relevance: Scaffolds work broadly; do not over-invest in fade logic. Principle-level lessons help most.

source: Belland et al. (2017) Bayesian network meta-analysis of scaffolding contexts
finding: Within-subject pre/post gains from scaffolding are strong across populations, STEM disciplines and assessment levels. Exceptions: inquiry-based learning, modeling visualization, and secondary education.
numbers: 56 studies; 20,000 MCMC samples; learners with learning disabilities g = 3.13.
limits: The g = 3.13 is pre-post, not controlled, so it is inflated. Few studies in that subgroup.
agent_relevance: Gains are largest for the weakest learners. A weaker model may gain more from lessons than a strong one.

source: Rosenshine & Meister (1994) Reciprocal teaching: a review of the research
finding: Reciprocal teaching (Palincsar & Brown) trains students to summarise, question, clarify and predict with the teacher fading out. Effect is large on researcher-made tests and small on standardised tests.
numbers: 16 studies, 1984-1992. Median effect size 0.88 on experimenter-made comprehension tests, 0.32 on standardised tests (from search-result summary of the abstract).
limits: Not opened. Galloway (2003) later found moderate effects and no gap between test types. The gap hints at teaching to the test.
agent_relevance: Gains on tests like the training task overstate transfer. Evaluate lessons on unlike problems (G3).

source: Cui & Sachan (2025) Investigating the Zone of Proximal Development of Language Models for In-Context Learning
finding: Treats in-context demonstrations as scaffolding. Sorts queries into three zones: solved by direct prompting, solved only with demonstrations (the model's ZPD), and unsolved even with demonstrations. Builds oracle demos by greedy search and predicts zones with an item-response model.
numbers: 8 LLaMA models (LLaMA-2 7B/13B, LLaMA-3 8B/70B, chat and base); datasets GSM8K and EZstance. KATE similarity retrieval lags oracle-demo accuracy by about 20% on average. For 6 of 8 models selective ICL dominates full ICL on the accuracy-cost plot.
limits: Oracle demos are an upper bound, not a usable method. Only two datasets. Each model has its own ZPD: easy items overlap across models, ZPD items do not. Two narrow-ZPD models (LLaMA-2-7b-chat, LLaMA-3-70B-Instruct) are hurt more by ICL.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct ZPD test for LLMs. Lessons help only for a middle band. Predict whether help applies before spending tokens, and expect some help to hurt.

source: Cui & Sachan (2025) ZPD-based curriculum for fine-tuning
finding: Training first on examples inside the model's ZPD gave faster convergence and better results than a random order in most cases. Learnability agrees between ICL and fine-tuning: unreachable examples are hardest, then ZPD, then easy ones.
numbers: LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, 6 epochs, GSM8K and EZstance. Exact gains shown only in figures; not extracted.
limits: Random order is a hard baseline in language modelling (Campos 2021), as the authors note. Accuracy gains not read from text.
agent_relevance: Useful lessons target near-solved problems, not trivial or impossible ones.

source: Liu, Yin, Lee & Chen (2024) Scaffolding language learning via multi-modal tutoring systems with pedagogical instructions
finding: GPT-4V tutors for children's image description were built on four theories, one being ZPD. Tutors with pedagogical instructions beat the plain tutor on every rubric dimension except modelling. The plain tutor gave direct answers; instructed tutors gave hints first.
numbers: Seven-dimension scaffolding rubric; two annotators, Cohen's kappa 0.75; simulated students at two proficiency levels.
limits: Simulated students, no real children. Scores are in a normalised figure; exact values not extracted.
agent_relevance: A plain model hands out answers; a scaffolded one withholds them. Fits our rule to give hints before answers.

source: Figueiredo (2025) A fuzzy logic prompting framework for LLMs in adaptive tasks (ZPD-based)
finding: A boundary prompt plus a JSON control schema with fuzzy scaffolding rules beat flat, few-shot and chain-of-thought prompts on scaffolding quality and adaptivity in simulated tutoring.
numbers: 4 models, 200 synthetic scenarios (100 math, 100 science, grades 6 and 8), four learner scaffold levels, 3 turns each. Scaffolding quality p < .001, d = 0.45 vs few-shot; adaptivity d = 0.46; grade match M = 4.42. Ablation: scaffold-only beat prompt-only d = 1.06 (p = 0.03).
limits: Scored by a GPT-4 judge, not humans. Scenarios made by GPT-4. Global Kruskal effect on grade match weak (p = 0.48). Not peer-reviewed.
agent_relevance: A rule table that picks support level from learner state helps. Judge bias is a risk (G5).

source: Wang et al. (2024) Tutor CoPilot, randomized controlled trial
finding: An LLM that gives expert-style suggestions to human tutors raised student mastery. Tutors using it asked more guiding questions and gave away answers less.
numbers: 900 tutors, 1,800 K-12 students; 7 weeks; exit-ticket pass rate 62% control to 66% treatment (+4 points, p<0.01); about $20 per tutor per year; 241,005 messages classified.
limits: Effects on participation points and student surveys were not significant. Some suggestions were not grade-appropriate. Human in the loop; math only.
agent_relevance: Scaffolding the helper, not the learner, scales expertise.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Tutor CoPilot: heterogeneity
finding: Benefit depended on tutor quality and experience: lower-rated and less experienced tutors gained most.
numbers: Up to +9 percentage points for lower-rated tutors versus +4 overall; conditional on attempting the exit ticket +3 points (p<0.05).
limits: Subgroup analysis in a preregistered study; multiple-hypothesis corrected p of 0.01 for the main pass rate.
agent_relevance: Help is worth most when base ability is weak.

source: Zhao, Hsu & Huang (2024) ZPD prompts for Chinese near-synonyms, via search result
finding: Prompts designed to make an LLM find the learner's ZPD before teaching Chinese near-synonyms.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Not opened; only listed in search results.
agent_relevance: Estimating the learner's level first is a design pattern.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion
finding: Agents write verbal reflections on feedback and store them in memory for later tries, with no weight update. A self-made lesson used as scaffold.
numbers: HumanEval pass@1 91% versus 80% for GPT-4.
limits: Abstract only. Coding with a test signal; reflection relies on real feedback.
agent_relevance: Direct template for lessons as scaffolds. Needs real failing output (G2).

source: Zhao et al. (2024) ExpeL: LLM agents are experiential learners
finding: Agent distils experience from training tasks into natural-language insights and retrieves them at test time without fine-tuning. Performance rises with accumulated experience and transfers.
numbers: No numbers in abstract; AAAI-24.
limits: Abstract only; no figures read.
agent_relevance: Lessons accumulate like a lasting scaffold across tasks.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager
finding: A skill library of verified code acts as a growing scaffold: earlier skills let the agent learn new tasks faster.
numbers: 3.3x more unique items, 2.3x longer distances, tech-tree milestones 15.3x faster than prior state of the art.
limits: Abstract only; Minecraft; skills verified by environment feedback.
agent_relevance: Store only lessons that passed a check.

source: Magister et al. (2023) Teaching small language models to reason
finding: A big teacher model's reasoning chains used to fine-tune a small student raised its accuracy.
numbers: T5 XXL on GSM8K from 8.11% to 21.99% using PaLM-540B chains.
limits: Fine-tuning, not scaffolding at inference; still far below the teacher.
agent_relevance: Teacher help transfers to a student, but the gain is bounded.

source: Jurewicz et al. (2024) LearnLM: improving Gemini for learning
finding: Pedagogical instruction following added to Gemini post-training; experts preferred it across learning scenarios.
numbers: Preference strength +31% over GPT-4o, +11% over Claude 3.5 Sonnet, +13% over Gemini 1.5 Pro.
limits: Abstract only. Expert preference, not measured learning. Author list not checked.
agent_relevance: Preference is not learning gain; do not count it as evidence for our agent.

source: Wass & Golding (2014) ZPD and scaffolding, via search summary
finding: A critique says scaffolding and ZPD are only partly alike at best, and superficially at worst.
numbers: None.
limits: Search snippet only; authors unconfirmed. Jiao & Lantolf (2021) also say the scaffolding metaphor is narrower than the ZPD.
agent_relevance: Do not call a scaffold ZPD-based just because it helps.

source: Kirschner, Sweller & Clark (2006) minimal-guidance critique, as summarised in Wikipedia Instructional scaffolding
finding: Cognitive-load critics say minimal guidance is inefficient for novices and that worked examples and practice help more.
numbers: Wikipedia also cites Hake (1998): under 30% recalled from a traditional physics lecture.
limits: Wikipedia page flagged for unreliable citations; Kirschner et al. not opened.
agent_relevance: Novices need strong guidance, experts less. Adapt help to level.

source: Wood, Bruner & Ross (1976): boundary case, 3-year-olds
finding: At age 3 the tutor had to step in most, and children often took apart their construction. Help beyond the learner's grasp did not carry over.
numbers: Four-block subtask: 0 of the 3-year-olds succeeded.
limits: Secondary source; no persistence figures given.
agent_relevance: Help beyond reach fails; matches the third zone in Cui & Sachan.
